nameStory: The Naked Ear Aeolid gets its unusual name from its distinctive finger-like projections called cerata, which look like tiny naked ears sticking up from its back. The word 'aeolid' comes from Aeolus, the Greek god of wind, referring to how these delicate sea slugs seem to dance in the ocean currents. Unlike many sea slugs that have protective coverings, this one's 'ears' are completely exposed.
description: The Naked Ear Aeolid is a tiny sea slug that belongs to a group called nudibranchs, which means 'naked gills.' These translucent marine creatures are typically less than an inch long and have rows of finger-like projections called cerata extending from their backs. They're soft-bodied mollusks without shells, gliding gracefully along underwater surfaces using their muscular foot. Their bodies are often translucent to whitish, allowing you to see internal structures through their skin.

idTips.label: Finger-like projections
idTips.description: Multiple rows of slender, finger-like cerata extend from the back, feeling soft and jelly-like to the touch, often with visible internal structures showing through translucent skin

idTips.label: Body color
idTips.description: Translucent to whitish body that may appear glassy or pearl-like when light passes through it, sometimes with subtle color variations

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small, typically under an inch long, requiring close observation to appreciate details of their delicate structure

idTips.label: Head tentacles
idTips.description: Two pairs of tentacles on the head - longer ones for sensing chemicals and shorter ones for touch, all feeling smooth and flexible

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides smoothly using a muscular foot, leaving no visible trail, often pausing to feed on small organisms

habitat: Found in shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines, typically in tide pools, under rocks, or on pier pilings. They prefer areas with good water circulation and often live near their hydroid prey - tiny colonial animals that look like miniature ferns growing on hard surfaces.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures begin to warm, often found in shallow tide pools during low tide explorations.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when they're easiest to spot in tide pools and shallow waters, feeding actively on hydroids.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to slightly deeper waters as temperatures cool, requiring more careful searching.
seasonality.winter: Least active period, typically found in deeper water or well-protected areas, rarely visible to casual observers.

funFact: These tiny sea slugs are solar-powered pirates - they steal photosynthetic cells from the hydroids they eat and keep them alive in their finger-like projections, essentially turning themselves into plant-animal hybrids that can make their own food from sunlight!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other small aeolid nudibranchs, but the Naked Ear Aeolid's translucent appearance and specific arrangement of cerata help distinguish it. Remember: if it looks like tiny transparent fingers reaching toward the light, you've likely found your naked-eared friend.
contextualKnowledge: Recent DNA analysis has shown that what scientists thought was one widespread species is actually several distinct species, with our New England Naked Ear Aeolid being different from similar-looking sea slugs in other parts of the Atlantic - a reminder that even tiny creatures can hold big surprises.
compareHints: Among its Tenellia relatives, the Naked Ear Aeolid is distinguished by its particularly translucent appearance and the arrangement of its cerata. The Green Aeolis has more obvious green coloration, while the Spotted Lagoon Aeolid shows distinct spots. DNA analysis is sometimes needed for definitive identification between closely related species in this genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relatives the Naked Ear Aeolid which lacks the vibrant green color, or the Spotted Lagoon Aeolid which has distinctive spots, the Green Aeolis maintains its solid green coloration throughout its body and cerata.
Unlike its relative the Green Aeolis which has a more uniform greenish coloration, the Spotted Lagoon Aeolid displays distinct dark spots on a translucent background.
Unlike the Green Aeolis which has a distinctly greenish coloration, Tenellia pustulata is more translucent with its characteristic bumpy texture.
Compared to the Green Aeolis (Tenellia viridis), this species shows more orange or golden coloration rather than green tones.
